strengths: Introduces ProstaTD, a new large-scale surgical triplet dataset for robot-assisted prostatectomy, extending triplet detection beyond cholecystectomy.
Provides dense per-frame bounding box annotations for instruments plus structured instrument-action-target triplet labels, enabling fully supervised triplet detection and localization.
Integrates three data sources (in-house, PSI-AVA, ESAD) and standardizes annotations, which could improve diversity relative to single-source CholecT50.
Defines clinically motivated temporal action boundaries for continuous and momentary actions, and introduces triplet-perspective tracking annotations.
Reports a substantial annotation effort with medical expert involvement and multiple verification rounds.
Benchmarks several modern detectors and proposes a YOLO-Triplet baseline, showing the feasibility of the detection task.
weaknesses: The central multi-source generalizability claim is not experimentally validated: no leave-one-source-out or cross-dataset evaluation is provided, and the test set mixes the same sources as training.
Annotation quality is not quantitatively validated: no inter-annotator agreement, annotation error rates, or human-audited accuracy statistics are reported for bounding boxes, actions, or targets.
The clinically defined temporal boundaries are asserted to reduce ambiguity but are not empirically evaluated, e.g., via boundary consistency, ablation, or comparison to alternative definitions.

Dataset reproducibility/access is insufficient: the paper says the dataset and code are available on Github but provides no link or anonymized access, and no dataset datasheet or detailed release plan.
Evaluation metrics are unclear and incomplete: mAP definitions for components versus triplets are not formally defined, and no triplet-class-level mAP or standard detection metric is reported.
Weakly supervised baselines (Tripnet-Det, RDV-Det) are evaluated under a bounding-box detection metric for which they are not designed, yielding near-zero scores and an unfair comparison.
The test set contains only five videos, which is small for a benchmark and may lead to high variance; no cross-validation or statistical significance analysis is provided.
A large fraction of instances involve null actions/targets, which inflates category and instance counts and may weaken the meaning of structured triplet detection.
The tracking section introduces a new triplet perspective but lacks main-paper baselines, metrics, and empirical validation; it is deferred to supplementary material without sufficient evidence.

The paper does not compare against existing triplet detection methods on CholecT50 or demonstrate cross-dataset transfer, making it difficult to assess the dataset's added value beyond annotation density.
Class imbalance and long-tail distribution are acknowledged but not addressed in evaluation, with no per-class or rare-triplet analysis beyond aggregate mAP.
Some claims of being 'first' and 'largest/most diverse' are not fully substantiated with a systematic comparison of all relevant surgical datasets or annotation quality.
Training details for baselines (hyperparameters, tuning, splits, augmentation) are largely absent, limiting reproducibility of the benchmark results.

strengths: The paper addresses real limitations of existing surgical triplet datasets: lack of dense spatial bounding boxes, ambiguous temporal boundaries, and single-source data.
It introduces a substantial annotated resource: 21 prostatectomy surgeries, 60,529 frames, 165,567 reported triplet instances, 7 instruments, 10 actions, 10 targets, and 89 triplet categories.
The annotation process involves clinical experts, multiple review rounds, ethical approval, informed consent, and a plan for non-commercial open release.
The paper provides baseline evaluations with several modern detectors and extends the dataset toward surgical instrument and triplet tracking.
weaknesses: No inter-annotator agreement or quantitative annotation-quality validation is reported, so claims of "high-precision" and clinically validated annotations are not empirically supported.

A large fraction of reported instances contain null actions and/or null targets (e.g., scissors,null,null; forceps,null,null), inflating the instance count and conflating meaningful triplets with idle or transition states.

The evaluation is not a standard triplet-detection evaluation: component-wise mAP and an unclear mAP_IVT are reported instead of mAP over full triplet classes with bounding boxes, and no per-class APs or annotation-ablation study is provided.
The multi-source generalizability claim is not directly tested; the train/val/test split is random rather than source-held-out, so cross-institution generalization is not evaluated.

The proposed YOLO-Triplet baseline is weak: it improves instrument mAP but degrades action/target mAP and only marginally improves IVT mAP over YOLOv10/v12; weakly supervised baselines are also weakly specified.
The tracking section is largely conceptual and lacks main-paper experiments; the proposed triplet tracking perspective is not validated, and comparison with CholecTrack20 is incomplete.
Novelty and scale are overstated: 21 videos is modest, ProstaTD has fewer triplet classes than CholecT50 (89 vs. 100), and much of the instance-count increase comes from null triplets.

Reproducibility and clarity issues remain: the actual dataset URL is missing, dataset names are inconsistent (ESAD/EASD), there are typos and duplicate/incorrect references, and key annotation protocol details are deferred to supplementary material.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale, multi-source surgical triplet detection dataset with dense bounding-box annotations, clinically grounded temporal boundaries, and multi-institutional prostatectomy videos, addressing clear limitations of existing benchmarks such as CholecT50.

The annotation protocol is described in substantial detail, involving surgeons and medically trained annotators, multiple review rounds, licensing considerations, and ethical safeguards, which supports the dataset's potential clinical relevance.
Provides a useful initial benchmark across weakly supervised and fully supervised detectors, including modern YOLO/DETR variants, and reports both accuracy and efficiency metrics.

The dataset captures complex multi-instrument prostatectomy scenes with high label concurrency, long-tail distributions, and explicit null/transition states, making it a potentially valuable resource for surgical video analysis.
The paper also includes tracking annotations under Intraoperative and proposed Triplet perspectives, extending beyond standard instrument-only tracking.
weaknesses: The evaluation does not convincingly isolate the claimed benefits of the dataset design: improvements from weak to full supervision are expected, but there is no controlled ablation showing that precise bounding boxes, standardized temporal boundaries, or multi-source data individually improve triplet detection or generalization.

The dataset is small in terms of procedures: 21 videos total, with only 5 test videos and 2 validation videos. This may produce high-variance results, and no cross-validation or per-source generalization analysis is provided despite the multi-source claim.

Annotation quality is not quantitatively validated: there is no inter-annotator agreement, no uncertainty analysis, and temporal boundary rules such as the 2-second criteria appear heuristic. The semi-automatic instrument annotation pipeline may introduce systematic bias.

Baseline implementation and evaluation details are unclear. It is not adequately explained how standard YOLO/DETR models produce action/target triplet mAPs, how component mAP is computed, or how matching is performed for triplet-level metrics, limiting reproducibility and fair comparison.

The tracking contribution is under-supported in the main paper: tracking baselines and detailed analyses are deferred to supplementary material, and the proposed Triplet Perspective is not empirically evaluated.

Several claims require qualification. ProstaTD is not clearly the largest by video/frame count or class diversity compared with existing triplet datasets, and the multi-institutional diversity is limited by the small number of surgeries and sources.
The handling of null actions/targets and category merging is not analyzed; these choices may substantially affect the task definition, class distribution, and evaluation results.

strengths: Introduces ProstaTD, a large-scale multi-institutional surgical triplet detection dataset with 71,775 frames and 196,490 triplet instances, including full bounding-box annotations and clinically defined temporal boundaries.

Moves the field from weak frame-level triplet classification toward fully supervised triplet detection, directly addressing key limitations of CholecT50 such as missing bounding boxes, unclear temporal boundaries, and single-institution bias.
Provides a rigorous annotation protocol with expert-defined triplet boundaries, multi-round review, and a reported average Cohen's kappa of 0.82 on sampled segments.

Releases two tailored annotation tools (Triplet-labelme and SurgLabel) and an evaluation toolkit (ivtdmetrics) that supports COCO-style mAP, IoU thresholds, per-component metrics, and video-wise evaluation.

Presents an extensive benchmark with weakly supervised, classical, transformer-based, YOLO-based, and surgical-specific methods, using five-fold cross-validation and reporting both frame-wise and video-wise metrics.
Proposes TDnet, a baseline with multi-task learning and instance-level self-distillation, which improves IVT detection over strong YOLO baselines and achieves competitive efficiency.
Includes an ethical statement describing IRB approval, informed consent, compensation, anonymization, and data-protection measures.
weaknesses: The dataset contains only 21 surgical videos/procedures, which is relatively small for claims of broad multi-institutional generalization; the large frame count may overstate diversity relative to the number of unique surgeries and surgeons.

The inter-rater agreement study covers only five 200-frame segments, about 1,000 frames or <1.5% of the dataset, and each segment was reviewed by only one surgeon, limiting the strength of annotation-quality validation.
Licensing and redistribution of derived PSI-AVA and ESAD videos/annotations are not fully clarified, and compatibility with the planned CC-BY-NC-SA-4.0 release should be explicitly established.
The benchmark shows severe class imbalance and low absolute performance: the best mAP_IVT@0.5 is only 36.1% and best F1 is 32.8%, indicating that the task remains far from solved in practice.

The proposed TDnet yields only modest gains over YOLOv12 (e.g., 1.8% mAP_IVT@0.5 and 1.3% mAP_IVT@0.50:0.95), and some per-class APs are worse than the baseline, so the method's contribution is limited.

Evaluation relies on five-fold cross-validation rather than a fixed held-out test split and does not include external validation on completely unseen institutions, which weakens benchmarking standardization.
Annotation used semi-automatic pre-labeling from a cystoscopic instrument detection model; although manually corrected, possible model-induced bias in initial bounding boxes is not analyzed.

Several strong claims, such as 'largest' and 'first,' require more careful qualification, since prior challenge datasets had non-public bounding-box test annotations and other large surgical datasets exist.
Reproducibility is affected by missing or blank URLs/repository links in the submitted manuscript, and some implementation details remain confined to appendices or configuration files.
There is no explicit analysis of annotation cost, error rates for bounding boxes and temporal boundaries, or consistency for rare triplet categories.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale surgical triplet dataset with dense bounding-box annotations, structured <instrument, verb, target> labels, and temporal boundaries, covering 71,775 frames and 196,490 instances across 21 videos.
Integrates multiple data sources (ESAD, PSI-AVA, and in-house PWH), which increases source-level variability relative to single-source surgical triplet datasets.
The annotation effort is substantial and involves medical experts; the reported Cohen's Kappa of 0.82 on sampled labels suggests reasonable label consistency, though the study is limited.
Provides annotation tools and an evaluation toolkit, which could be useful community resources if actually released and documented.
Benchmarks a broad set of detection models, including classical detectors, modern YOLO variants, DETR-based models, and task-specific surgical methods.
Clearly identifies limitations of prior surgical triplet datasets, especially the lack of bounding boxes and inconsistent temporal boundaries in CholecT50.
Defines the task, data format, and evaluation metrics in a mostly clear manner, and includes an ethical statement and reproducibility statement.
The proposed TDnet baseline attempts to address triplet class imbalance via multi-task learning and self-distillation, which is a reasonable direction for this setting.
weaknesses: The central generalization claim is not supported by the evaluation. The five-fold cross-validation randomly mixes videos from all sources, so it does not test cross-institution or cross-source generalization, which is exactly what the multi-source dataset is claimed to enable.

The temporal-boundary contribution is largely unevaluated. The benchmark is still frame-wise triplet detection and provides no temporal localization metric, boundary agreement analysis, or downstream benefit from the claimed clinically defined temporal boundaries.

The inter-rater agreement study is weak and does not actually measure inter-rater agreement: only five 200-frame segments are used, each reviewed by a single surgeon against the consolidated ground truth, with no multiple raters on the same segment and no agreement analysis for bounding boxes or temporal boundaries.

Reproducibility and release claims are difficult to verify. The manuscript states that code, dataset, annotation tools, and evaluation toolkit are available at an anonymous repository, but the relevant links are missing or blank in the submitted text.

The dataset contains many null/null triplets and heavily merged label categories (e.g., merging prostate apex/DVC into prostate and vas deferens into seminal vesicle). This may inflate instance counts, reduce clinical granularity, and make the triplet definition ambiguous for meaningful instrument-action-target interactions.

The benchmark comparisons lack statistical significance testing. TDnet's gains over strong detectors are modest and often within one standard deviation, so the claim of improved performance is not convincingly supported.

The proposed TDnet method is incremental and under-ablated. It combines multi-task learning and self-distillation, but lacks comparisons to simpler alternatives such as focal loss, class-balanced sampling, or other imbalance-handling strategies, as well as sensitivity analyses for key hyperparameters.

The evaluation does not adequately validate the dataset's practical utility. There is no cross-source or leave-one-institution-out benchmark, no analysis of source-specific shortcuts, and no evidence that models trained on ProstaTD transfer better than models trained on existing datasets.

Table 1 may conflate different annotation types across datasets, such as instrument/bbox instances versus triplet instances. This makes the 'largest' claim less comparable than presented, and ProstaTD actually has fewer triplet classes than CholecT50.

The method-specific comparisons are not fully fair or transparent. Weakly supervised baselines are expected to perform poorly, and adaptations of TAPIR and MCIT-IG are not described in sufficient detail to assess comparability.

Annotation quality control is not sufficiently quantified. The paper reports multiple review rounds and expert involvement, but gives no annotation error rates, bounding-box quality statistics, temporal-boundary consistency, or detailed breakdown of disagreements.

Several claims are overstated or imprecise, such as being the first fully supervised surgical triplet detection dataset/task and achieving the best results across all major components, when TDnet is not best on all reported metrics and prior detection-style benchmarks exist.

The paper does not clearly investigate how rare triplet classes and class imbalance affect evaluation reliability. AP over many extremely rare triplet categories may be unstable, yet the benchmark presents aggregate mAP without sufficient per-class support or uncertainty analysis.

Ethical and licensing handling is mentioned but not fully resolved. In particular, patient consent for releasing the in-house PWH videos, the compatibility of re-releasing combined public datasets under a single license, and the enforceability of the stated use restrictions are not fully clarified.

strengths: Introduces ProstaTD, a large-scale fully supervised surgical triplet detection dataset with 71,775 frames, 196,490 annotated instances, 89 triplet classes, dense bounding boxes, and clinically defined temporal boundaries.
The dataset is multi-institutional/multi-source (PWH, PSI-AVA, ESAD), providing more diversity than prior triplet datasets such as CholecT50 and supporting more realistic benchmarking.

The annotation protocol is clinically grounded, involves many expert contributors, includes multiple verification rounds, reports strong inter-rater agreement (average Cohen's kappa 0.82), and addresses ethical/privacy requirements.
Releases practical resources beyond the dataset: two tailored annotation tools and the ivtdmetrics evaluation toolkit, which supports mAP@50, mAP@50:95, component metrics, and video-wise evaluation.

Provides a comprehensive benchmark with five-fold cross-validation, multiple baseline families (weakly supervised, classical detectors, modern YOLO/DETR, surgical-specific methods), ablation studies, confusion matrix analysis, and per-class AP analysis.

Proposes TDnet as a tailored baseline, combining multi-task learning and instance-level self-distillation to mitigate class imbalance, achieving the best overall performance on the main triplet detection metric.
The paper is well structured, reproducible, and includes sufficient implementation details, dataset statistics, and evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: The dataset is limited to robot-assisted radical prostatectomy with 21 videos and 89 triplet classes; although large in annotated instances, it is narrower in procedure and class coverage than CholecT50, so generalization to other surgical procedures remains unverified.

Temporal boundaries are emphasized as a key contribution, but the benchmark does not explicitly evaluate temporal boundary accuracy or temporal triplet detection; evaluation remains frame-level/video-wise detection.
Bounding-box annotation quality is not quantitatively validated; the inter-rater study focuses on triplet labels only and uses a relatively small sample of five 200-frame segments.
TDnet's improvements over strong YOLO baselines are modest (e.g., mAP_IVT@0.5: 36.1% vs. 34.3%) and are reported with standard deviations that suggest the gains may not be statistically significant.
The paper re-annotates videos from public datasets (PSI-AVA and ESAD), but licensing and derivative-work compliance are discussed only briefly.

The severe long-tail distribution and low absolute triplet detection performance (F1 around 33%) indicate that important practical triplet detection remains difficult and may limit immediate downstream deployment.

Weakly supervised baselines are not directly comparable to fully supervised detectors, so their extremely low performance mainly illustrates the supervision gap rather than establishing competitive baselines.
